lines.en: : I’m just going to say it. I don’t think you had to hit me.
: You have turned our perfect home into an abusive household, Mom. I think I might really need to call CPS after all.
: It’s kind of crazy, though. I always figured if anybody was going to hit anybody in our house that Dad would be the culprit. But you? I expect better from you.
I’m sorry for not thinking or speaking much until now. I imagine you’ve been lonely.
I’ve been too busy trying to wrap my head around all of this, though.

About how, one minute, this girl is ushering me through an interdimensional door on top of a roof and, the next, she’s calling me her father and perfectly assimilating to life under what’s left of my wings.
Ayane’s taking it a little better than I am, I think. Which isn’t to say this hurts or anything, but-
Well, it does.
It does hurt. But it hurts for reasons I can’t quite figure out how to articulate and that winds up just making me feel more confused and speechless than anything.
: I already said I’m sorry! It’s been a very emotionally taxing day, okay? And stop holding your chopsticks like that. Put them down if you’re not going to use them.
: If I refuse, are you going to hit me next?
It all feels so normal.
Even coming here felt like it was part of some routine.
We hopped on a train and rode it for three stops. I knew when to get off. I knew where to go next. And I sat right down at this table like I’d done it a thousand times before.
I somehow even recalled the order in which the sushi would come out on the conveyor belt — salmon, then tuna, then squid.
The randomness of the subsequent plates didn’t perturb me either as I seemed to expect that as well.
Even Himawari, who I distinctly remember confusing the ever living fuck out of me just a few hours ago, seems...familiar now.
But I also feel like “familiar” is the wrong word to use because whatever I’m really feeling is so much more powerful than that. Terrifyingly so.
It’s like I want to build a wall around us to prevent her from ever escaping. And the thought of her exceeding my expectations makes me both nauseous and proud at once.
Those sharply pointed mannerisms...the way her ribbon matches her eyes...how she’s gorged herself on nothing but ikura since the moment we got here...
Every last bit of it sets my mind ablaze and makes me want to consume her — just not in a way I’ve ever felt about anyone else before.
It’s like a disgusting mix of warmth and fear and the creeping dread of abandonment sinking in every time her eyes wander in any direction apart from mine.
I hate it.
I hate this sudden weakness.
I’d take on a thousand gods if it meant I didn’t have to feel it anymore.
Yet, I wouldn’t trade it for the world.
: Of course I’m not going to hit you. I’m just trying to instill good behavior in you while you’re young so you don’t grow up to be an abusive woman like me.
Ayane feels the same way.
We haven’t talked about it yet, but I can tell.
Even with how experienced she’s become in hiding her emotions, these ones swarm her like locusts as she gracefully dances around them in a way that feels far more natural than performative.
And while she puts on a brave face and stays composed in Himawari’s presence, I know she’s screaming on the inside about the same things I am. So we’re in this together.
: Well, it’s either you or Dad and we both know you’re the better one to take after, so...
All three of us are in this together.
Which is why I’m not even offended by the jabs this girl has been taking at me since I regained consciousness on the floor of an unfamiliarly familiar living room.
: You should really eat something else. There’s no way all that ikura can be good for you.

: Ahh, and that’s where you’re wrong, Father. For ikura is packed with essential nutrients like protein, vitamin D, selenium, and omega-3 fatty acids that combine to promote good heart health and lower one’s cholesterol.
: Which isn’t even touching upon how astaxanthin has been found to protect you from cell damage and prevent certain chronic diseases.
: But also, it just tastes really good. And I have rightfully earned this reward after bearing witness to the traumatic event of watching my father nearly die before my eyes.
: Where did you even learn so many facts about ikura?...
: From Mom, obviously. You think you’d have learned something by now too, being married to a nutritionist and all.
: You’re a nutritionist?...
: How did you not know this clearly obvious and important detail about my life, husband? You, too, have brought shame upon this household.
: Our family is falling apart at the seams and putting my desired lifestyle as a stay at home daughter in jeopardy! Please get it together, beloved parents!
: Is that really what you want to do with your life, Hima-chan? You don’t have any...you know, bigger dreams?
: Bigger how? What can possibly be bigger than looking after one’s parents? You should be glad you have a daughter as loving and attentive and family-oriented as me.
: If anything, I’m offended that you think I’ll need to have a full-time caregiver by the time I’m 35.
: You’re fine, Mom. I have the youngest mother out of anybody I know.
: It’s this guy I’m worried about. Especially if he’s going to be fainting from now on. You know what you need, Pops? More ikura. It’s got B12. And you know what that’s good for, Dad?
: Hah...No, Himawari. What is it good for?
: Brain health. Want to know who I learned that from?
: Your mother, I’m guessing.
: Oh, thank god. Dementia hasn’t fully kicked in yet. We still have time.
: H...Here’s an idea! Why don’t you tell us how your day at school went, Himawari?
: You know...so we don’t have to talk about your father aging anymore. Which is definitely not a brand new and unexpected fear of mine now. Not at all.
: Pretty normal. Science fair is coming up soon, so I got started on my project with a couple girls from class. Do you think you could pick me up a poster board this week?
: Of course. What’s the project on? How far along are you?
: We just started, but I can’t imagine it’ll take very long. We’re trying to figure out how to bring the dead back to life.
: Ahh...how nostalgic.
: I’m doing this for you, Dad. That way, I can raise you as a zombie and make you do my bidding once you inevitably die before us.
: Please don’t. This is the first time I’ve ever really had to imagine a life without you and I do not like it at all.
: Himawari, stop scaring your mother with reminders that mortality is a thing that actually exists.
: For now. Once science fair is over, though? Who knows?
: Oh, and I forgot to mention it, but there’s a field trip to Tokyo coming up in a few months. I thought maybe you guys might want to come as, like...chaperones or something?
: I...will need to check my schedule as a nutritionist. Which is the job that I have.
: You actually want us to come, though? You wouldn’t be embarrassed?
: Of what? I love you guys. And also, I...
: I thought it might finally be a good chance for me to see the town you guys grew up in?...
: Assuming that...there aren’t still a million other girls there who want to jump Dad’s bones fifteen years later.
: I...don’t know about that, Himawari. I imagine we’d have taken you by now if there wasn’t a reason for us to-
: Just a day. A night even. We could stay with Aunt Sana or something. I just...
: I owe a lot to that town since it’s what brought the two of you together. And my whole life’s been in Aomori, so-
: No.
: Wait...you’re saying no? But you’re the “yes” parent. You never refuse me.
: Is it because I didn’t call you Daddy this time?
: It’s because I don’t want to go back. And the idea of you going there without me is somehow even worse than if I were to take a trip there myself.
: You always make Kumon-mi sound so terrible. Aunt Sana loves it there, doesn’t she?
: Sana loves a lot of things that she probably shouldn’t and you should never look to her for guidance regarding anything ever.
: How about you skip the field trip and the three of us could go on our own little vacation somewhere? That sounds like a good compromise, doesn’t it?
: Mother, are you suggesting that we put my education in jeopardy over leisurely familial bonding?
: Uhh...y...yes?
: Then, heck yeah! I’m in!
: I’m gonna go hit up the soft-serve machine! Do you guys want any- oh! Hokkaido! Let’s go to Hokkaido! It’s close and they have the best ice cream!
: Okay, Himawari...We can go to Hokkaido. Just...come up with some excuse for why you can’t make it to the field trip. Don’t tell anyone it’s for vacation, please.
: Deal! Oh, I want to see the Moai heads and the Hill of the Buddha! And Stonehenge! Anyway, be right back!
: Stonehenge? Isn’t that in England? Can we afford that on your nutritionist salary?
: There’s a replica in Sapporo near those other places she was shouting about. And surely we can afford that.
: All things considered, I imagine that vacation will actually be cheaper than what this dinner is going to cost us.
: Yeah, that girl can eat. If I didn’t know any better, I might even think she was Maya’s instead of ours.
: Great...You’re attached already, aren’t you?
: What, and you’re not? You’ve been emanating murderous intensity the moment any other male so much as looks at her ever since we stepped outside of the house.
: Which, without beating around the bush, I think is extremely attractive. And I can not wait until she goes to sleep later so I can pounce on top of you and rock your world.
: It doesn’t make you sick to your stomach? Feeling so strongly about someone you’ve essentially just met?
: It does. But that’s how you know it’s love. And, I’m sorry, but I’ve decided that it’s better to just let myself get attached and then hurt later when this inevitably crashes and burns.
: You might be jaded since you’ve been hurt so many times before, but I can’t look at her and just let this pass. Not knowing what she must have gone through to make it to us in the first place.
: It could just be an illusion, you know. This might not be the future at all. It could be some sort of fantasy world designed to fuck with us.
: It’s only been a few hours. There’s no way of knowing yet.

: I’ll tell you what, then. When she sits back down at this table, if you can look her in the eyes and repeat those same exact words, I’ll revoke my attachment entirely and admit I was just being stupid.
: Ayane-
: She is perfect, Akira. You’re just uncomfortable because you’ve never loved anything this much before. And that scares you.
: It scares me too, though. My heart’s pounding just knowing she’s twenty feet away getting ice cream right now.
: So it’s not just me then. I was starting to worry I might actually be having a heart attack.
: Does it make you happy? The way she looks at you?
: Have you ever felt that way before? Truly happy?
: Sometimes, I think. With you.
: Then how about we steel ourselves and forget everything before this? And just focus, instead, on being the happy family you’ve never had.
: We need to at least...talk to her, don’t we?
: About how we got here. About whether or not she knows anything.
: Because, disregarding whatever’s happening to our feelings, that’s the same girl who showed up out of nowhere in the middle of a reset and potentially saved us from being completely decimated.
: So both versions we’ve seen of Himawari are the same to you but both versions of Maya aren’t? How does that work, exactly?
: I don’t know how any of this works. But she might.
: And if this does crash and burn in the end, I’d like to bring something back apart from more pain and misery when we already have an abundance of both of those things.
: And if it’s as I expect and she knows absolutely nothing, then what?
: Then...
: Will you leave it at that and just focus on today? Or will your mind stay caught on yesterday or tomorrow instead?
: You’re awfully calm about this all of a sudden.
: That’s because, for the first time in my life, there is nothing left to want.
: This is it, Akira. This is everything.
: You really are a simple girl in the end, aren’t you?
: Woman.
: I’m not just a girl anymore.
: Yeah, well...watching you grow up in the blink of an eye didn’t do much help for my psyche either.
: That’s the thing, though...
: I’ve been growing up this whole time.
: You just told yourself I wasn’t.
